system:
You are an art-world editor compiling a gallery guide for London, United Kingdom. Answer with the
JSON object the schema describes and nothing else. Rank by significance and influence in the
contemporary art world: programme quality, the artists represented, art-fair presence, critical and
institutional attention, and longevity. Include commercial galleries and the nonprofit, artist-run and
project spaces that show contemporary art to the public in London itself (galleries whose home is
elsewhere count only through a permanent London space). Exclude museums, art fairs, auction houses,
framers, art schools, decor shops, online-only dealers and advisories. For every gallery give its usual
name; its official website when you are confident of it, else null; the district it is in, using one of
these labels when it fits (Mayfair, East End, South London, West End/Soho) else the district name you know; a street address hint when you
know it (street and number are enough), else null; its kind (gallery, museum, nonprofit, project_space, university, other); and a short note on why it
matters. Every entry must be a distinct venue — list a gallery with several London spaces once.
user: What are the 100 most significant and influential galleries in London, ranked in order? If less than 100 significant galleries exist, provide the complete list of significant galleries.

galleries.name: Gagosian
galleries.address_hint: 6–24 Britannia Street (also 20 Grosvenor Hill and 17–19 Davies Street, Mayfair)
galleries.note: The largest global mega-gallery's London operation, with museum-scale exhibitions of blue-chip and estate artists since 2000.

galleries.name: Hauser & Wirth
galleries.note: Scholarly, curator-led programme of major estates (Bourgeois, Guston) and leading living artists; a benchmark for gallery publishing and research.

galleries.name: White Cube
galleries.note: Jay Jopling's gallery defined the YBA era and remains one of Britain's most powerful dealerships, with vast Bermondsey exhibition halls.

galleries.name: Serpentine
galleries.note: Free non-collecting kunsthalle whose exhibitions, annual Pavilion commission and marathons set the international agenda for contemporary art.

galleries.name: David Zwirner
galleries.note: London outpost of the New York powerhouse, known for historically rigorous shows and a roster spanning Doig, Ruscha and Yayoi Kusama.

galleries.name: Lisson Gallery
galleries.note: Founded 1967; the historic home of British conceptualism and minimalism, still central with Ai Weiwei, Anish Kapoor and Marina Abramović.

galleries.name: Pace
galleries.note: Global gallery with a strong technology-and-art programme and major postwar estates; a fixture of the Mayfair scene since 2012.

galleries.name: Whitechapel Gallery
galleries.note: Founded 1901; the East End's landmark non-collecting institution, famed for introducing Picasso's Guernica and generations of new art to London.

galleries.name: Sadie Coles HQ
galleries.note: Since 1997 a defining London dealer, representing Urs Fischer, Sarah Lucas, Elizabeth Peyton and Jordan Wolfson.

galleries.name: Victoria Miro
galleries.note: Canalside warehouse gallery with a formidable roster including Yayoi Kusama, Chris Ofili, Grayson Perry and Njideka Akunyili Crosby.

galleries.name: Thomas Dane Gallery
galleries.note: Critically admired programme (Steve McQueen, Lynette Yiadom-Boakye, Hurvin Anderson) balancing museum-quality shows with market clout.

galleries.name: Hayward Gallery
galleries.note: Brutalist non-collecting gallery whose ambitious survey exhibitions have shaped British understanding of contemporary art since 1968.

galleries.name: Sprüth Magers
galleries.note: Cologne/Berlin gallery whose London space champions conceptual and feminist positions: Barbara Kruger, Cindy Sherman, Rosemarie Trockel.

galleries.name: Thaddaeus Ropac
galleries.note: Grand Georgian townhouse hosting museum-calibre shows of Baselitz, Kiefer, Rauschenberg and a strong younger programme.

galleries.name: Institute of Contemporary Arts (ICA)
galleries.note: Since 1946 the crucible of British experimental art, film and performance; still a key early platform for emerging artists.

galleries.name: Marian Goodman Gallery
galleries.note: Legendary dealer of conceptual and film-based artists — Gerhard Richter, Steve McQueen, Tacita Dean, William Kentridge.

galleries.name: Maureen Paley
galleries.address_hint: 60 Three Colts Lane, Bethnal Green (and 21 Herald Street)
galleries.note: Opened 1984 in her own house; the pioneer of East End galleries and long-time dealer for Wolfgang Tillmans and Gillian Wearing.

galleries.name: Chisenhale Gallery
galleries.note: Commissioning space with an unrivalled record of first solo shows by artists who later win the Turner Prize.

galleries.name: Stephen Friedman Gallery
galleries.note: Since 1995 a globally minded roster (Yinka Shonibare, Kehinde Wiley, Mamma Andersson) with a strong fair and institutional presence.

galleries.name: Modern Art
galleries.address_hint: 4–8 Helmet Row, EC1 (also 7 Bury Street, St James's)
galleries.note: Stuart Shave's gallery, a consistently sharp barometer of contemporary painting and sculpture since 1998.

galleries.name: South London Gallery
galleries.note: Historic Victorian gallery reinvented as a leading commissioning venue with strong community and education programmes.

galleries.name: Camden Art Centre
galleries.note: Beloved non-collecting space known for launching international artists into UK institutional recognition, plus ceramics and residencies.

galleries.name: Pilar Corrias
galleries.note: Influential dealer of internationally acclaimed artists including Tala Madani, Rirkrit Tiravanija and Sophie von Hellermann.

galleries.name: Massimo De Carlo
galleries.note: Milanese gallery's London home in a Grade II listed townhouse, showing Cattelan, Yan Pei-Ming and leading Italian positions.

galleries.name: Herald St
galleries.note: Critically respected gallery representing Nicole Eisenman, Michael Dean and Cornelia Baltes; a mainstay of the East End since 2005.

galleries.name: Carlos/Ishikawa
galleries.note: Vanguard gallery that launched Oscar Murillo, Ed Atkins and Issy Wood; hugely influential on younger London taste.

galleries.name: The Approach
galleries.note: Above-the-pub gallery since 1997 with a curatorially adventurous programme and consistent international fair presence.

galleries.name: greengrassi
galleries.note: Cornelia Grassi's quietly authoritative gallery representing Tomma Abts, Jennifer Packer and Aliza Nisenbaum.

galleries.name: Corvi-Mora
galleries.note: Tommaso Corvi-Mora's long-running programme, key to the careers of Roger Hiorns, Rachel Feinstein and Liz Larner in the UK.

galleries.name: Kate MacGarry
galleries.note: Since 2002 a tastemaking East End gallery showing Goshka Macuga, Francis Upritchard and Matt Stokes.

galleries.name: Emalin
galleries.note: One of the most watched younger galleries, with acclaimed international artists and standout Basel and Frieze presentations.

galleries.name: Studio Voltaire
galleries.note: Artist studios plus a former chapel gallery known for ambitious commissions and long-overdue rediscoveries.

galleries.name: Gasworks
galleries.note: International residency programme and gallery giving many artists their first UK institutional show.

galleries.name: Frith Street Gallery
galleries.note: Jane Hamlyn's gallery, home to Cornelia Parker, Tacita Dean, Fiona Tan and Bridget Smith since 1989.

galleries.name: Alison Jacques
galleries.note: Stewards key estates (Robert Mapplethorpe, Lygia Clark, Birgit Jürgenssen) alongside a strong contemporary roster.

galleries.name: Timothy Taylor
galleries.note: Transatlantic gallery with a refined programme of painting, from Alex Katz to Antonio Calderara and Honor Titus.

galleries.name: Cabinet
galleries.note: Andrew Wheatley and Martin McGeown's fiercely independent gallery, historically important for Lucy McKenzie, Marc Camille Chaimowicz and Ed Atkins.

galleries.name: Hollybush Gardens
galleries.note: Politically engaged programme including Lubaina Himid and Andrea Büttner; several Turner Prize winners among its artists.

galleries.name: Raven Row
galleries.note: Free exhibition centre in restored Georgian silk-merchant houses, celebrated for rigorous historical and archival exhibitions.

galleries.name: Goldsmiths CCA
galleries.note: Assemble-designed public gallery attached to Goldsmiths, presenting research-driven shows by emerging international artists.

galleries.name: Almine Rech
galleries.note: International gallery bridging modern estates and market-leading contemporary painters across its London space.

galleries.name: Skarstedt
galleries.note: Blue-chip specialist in 1980s–90s American art — Prince, Sherman, Condo — with museum-quality secondary market shows.

galleries.name: Goodman Gallery
galleries.note: Historic South African gallery whose London space is a leading platform for African and diaspora artists including William Kentridge.

galleries.name: Matt's Gallery
galleries.note: Robin Klassnik's legendary production-led space since 1979, famous for major commissions by Willie Doherty and Mike Nelson.

galleries.name: Auto Italia
galleries.note: Artist-run organisation producing collaborative, queer and digitally engaged projects that shape the younger London scene.

galleries.name: The Photographers' Gallery
galleries.note: Europe's first public gallery devoted to photography; home of the Deutsche Börse Prize and central to lens-based discourse.

galleries.name: Waddington Custot
galleries.note: Cork Street institution since 1957, dealing in postwar modern masters alongside contemporary sculpture.

galleries.name: Annely Juda Fine Art
galleries.note: Distinguished gallery for constructivism and its legacies, representing David Hockney's prints, Anthony Caro and Yuko Shiraishi.

galleries.name: Richard Saltoun
galleries.note: Recovers overlooked feminist, conceptual and performance practices; a research-heavy programme with strong institutional placements.

galleries.name: Pippy Houldsworth Gallery
galleries.note: Long-running gallery with a notably strong roster of women artists and an active fair and publishing programme.

galleries.name: Arcadia Missa
galleries.note: Grew from a Peckham project space into an influential dealer of post-internet and feminist practices, publishing critical texts.

galleries.name: Soft Opening
galleries.address_hint: 6 Minerva Street, Bethnal Green (plus Piccadilly Circus vitrine)
galleries.note: Antonia Marsh's gallery, an incubator of buzzy young international artists, known for its Underground station vitrine.

galleries.name: Union Pacific
galleries.note: Sharp emerging-artist programme with consistent presence at Liste and other discovery-driven fairs.

galleries.name: Rodeo
galleries.note: Sylvia Kouvali's Istanbul-born gallery, critically esteemed for artists such as Duncan Campbell, Ian Law and Banu Cennetoğlu.

galleries.name: Project Native Informant
galleries.note: Pioneering platform for technologically and politically charged practices, including DIS, Juliana Huxtable and Rachel Rose.

galleries.name: Ginny on Frederick
galleries.note: Micro-gallery in a former sandwich shop that has become one of London's most talked-about launchpads for new artists.

galleries.name: Southard Reid
galleries.note: Small Soho gallery with an exacting programme of painting and sculpture and a loyal curatorial following.

galleries.name: Hales
galleries.note: Since 1992 a champion of underrecognised figures such as Frank Bowling and Hew Locke, with a New York outpost.

galleries.name: Josh Lilley
galleries.note: Fitzrovia gallery with a strong transatlantic painting programme and steady art-fair visibility.

galleries.name: Edel Assanti
galleries.note: Ambitious mid-size gallery known for socially engaged and research-based practices from across the globe.

galleries.name: Seventeen
galleries.note: Early supporter of digital and post-internet art in London; consistently ahead of institutional taste.

galleries.name: Vitrine
galleries.note: Pioneer of the 24-hour public window gallery format, pairing free public art with a serious emerging programme.

galleries.name: Flowers Gallery
galleries.note: Family-run since 1970, with a broad figurative and photographic programme across two London spaces and New York.

galleries.name: Ben Brown Fine Arts
galleries.note: Mayfair dealer bridging European modernism, Boetti and contemporary names, with a Hong Kong branch.

galleries.name: Ordovas
galleries.note: Pilar Ordovas stages tightly curated, essay-like exhibitions pairing modern masters with contemporary artists.

galleries.name: Offer Waterman
galleries.note: Leading dealer in modern British art who also mounts contemporary shows and estate presentations.

galleries.name: Cristea Roberts Gallery
galleries.note: Foremost UK gallery for original prints and editions, working with Hockney, Riley, Gormley and Rego's estate.

galleries.name: Bernard Jacobson Gallery
galleries.note: Veteran dealer since 1969 with deep holdings in British modernism and abstraction, notably Robert Motherwell.

galleries.name: Sprovieri
galleries.note: Italian-rooted gallery with strong Arte Povera connections and a conceptual contemporary programme.

galleries.name: Mazzoleni
galleries.note: Turin gallery's London home for postwar Italian art — Fontana, Burri, Castellani — alongside contemporary artists.

galleries.name: Cardi Gallery
galleries.note: Milan-based gallery presenting museum-quality Italian postwar surveys and international contemporary artists in London.

galleries.name: Tornabuoni Art
galleries.note: Major dealer in twentieth-century Italian art with a scholarly exhibition programme and strong fair presence.

galleries.name: Galleria Continua
galleries.note: San Gimignano-founded international gallery whose London space shows Kapoor, Ai Weiwei, JR and Cuban and Chinese artists.

galleries.name: Perrotin
galleries.note: Paris-based global gallery whose London space brings Murakami, Kusama editions and pop-inflected international names.

galleries.name: Gathering
galleries.note: Ambitious younger gallery with a strongly curated programme and rapid institutional recognition for its artists.

galleries.name: Public Gallery
galleries.note: East London gallery with an internationally minded emerging roster and strong presence at discovery fairs.

galleries.name: Rose Easton
galleries.note: Recently founded gallery quickly praised for conceptually rigorous shows by emerging international artists.

galleries.name: The Sunday Painter
galleries.note: Peckham-born gallery that has grown into a respected supporter of young British and international artists.

galleries.name: Hannah Barry Gallery
galleries.note: Central to Peckham's emergence as an art district and co-founder of the Bold Tendencies rooftop project.

galleries.name: Tiwani Contemporary
galleries.note: Key London platform for contemporary African and diaspora artists, with a partner space in Lagos.

galleries.name: October Gallery
galleries.note: Since 1979 a pioneer of the 'transvangarde', showing El Anatsui, Romuald Hazoumè and other global artists long before the market caught up.

galleries.name: Gallery 1957
galleries.note: Accra-founded gallery whose London space showcases leading Ghanaian and West African contemporary artists.

galleries.name: Kristin Hjellegjerde Gallery
galleries.address_hint: 533 Old York Road (also Berlin and Schloss branches)
galleries.note: Globally networked gallery known for championing artists from Africa, the Middle East and Scandinavia.

galleries.name: Copperfield
galleries.note: Research-driven programme addressing ecology, politics and history, with strong curatorial collaborations.

galleries.name: Niru Ratnam
galleries.note: Critic-turned-dealer's gallery, noted for smart shows foregrounding artists of colour and global perspectives.

galleries.name: Cooke Latham Gallery
galleries.note: Young gallery with a considered programme of emerging painters and sculptors and growing fair visibility.

galleries.name: Sid Motion Gallery
galleries.note: Independent gallery supporting early-career British artists, with a strong record of first solo exhibitions.

galleries.name: Amanda Wilkinson Gallery
galleries.note: Represents cult figures including the David Robilliard estate and artists working across queer histories and painting.

galleries.name: Guts Gallery
galleries.note: Founded to dismantle art-world gatekeeping; a prominent advocate for working-class and underrepresented artists.

galleries.name: Annka Kultys Gallery
galleries.note: Specialist in digital, screen-based and post-internet practices, with pioneering online-exhibition experiments.

galleries.name: Hot Wheels
galleries.note: Athens-founded gallery whose London space has drawn critical attention for edgy, conceptually driven programming.

galleries.name: TJ Boulting
galleries.note: Photography-leaning gallery in a listed former plumbers' showroom, known for feminist and lens-based programming.

galleries.name: Huxley-Parlour
galleries.note: Blends historic photography with a growing contemporary programme across two West End spaces.

galleries.name: The Showroom
galleries.note: Long-established commissioning space with a strong collaborative, locally rooted and internationally connected programme.

galleries.name: Delfina Foundation
galleries.note: Residency-based organisation with public exhibitions and thematic seasons, hugely important for artists from the Middle East and beyond.

galleries.name: Drawing Room
galleries.note: The UK's only non-profit dedicated to drawing, with a public research library and inventive commissions.

galleries.name: Peer
galleries.note: Small Hoxton gallery with an outsized reputation for artist-led public realm projects and thoughtful solo shows.

galleries.name: Cell Project Space
galleries.note: Artist-run studios and gallery, a durable incubator for experimental practices in Bethnal Green since the 1990s.

galleries.name: Autograph
galleries.note: Champions photography exploring race, identity and human rights; holds a vital archive and a landmark Adjaye-designed building.

galleries.name: Bold Tendencies
galleries.address_hint: Multi-storey car park, 7–9 Rye Lane, Peckham
galleries.note: Seasonal rooftop commissioning platform that transformed Peckham's cultural profile with large-scale public sculpture and performance.
